title: Cation Exchange Capacity and Nutrient Buffering
objective: Interpret cation exchange capacity as one part of root-zone buffering and avoid using it as a stand-alone fertility score.

terms.definition: Positively charged ion such as K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, or NH4+.
Negatively charged surface position that can reversibly hold a cation.
Quantity of exchangeable cations a material can hold under a defined test method.
Proportion of exchange sites occupied by selected base cations; interpretation is soil- and method-dependent.

coreScience: Clay minerals and organic materials carry surface charges that can attract and exchange cations. CEC influences how strongly a root zone buffers changes in potassium, calcium, magnesium, ammonium, and other positively charged nutrients. It does not directly hold anions such as nitrate in the same way.

CEC depends on material identity and, for variable-charge surfaces, pH. Peat, coir, vermiculite, clay, and many composts can have meaningful exchange capacity; perlite, sand, and rockwool have relatively little. Reported values are method-dependent and should not be copied between laboratories without context.

A high-CEC medium can buffer supply but can also retain an unbalanced history. A low-CEC inert medium can perform well when solution composition and irrigation are controlled precisely. Buffering changes the management strategy; it does not rank one system as universally superior.
cultivationRelevance: In coir, initial potassium, sodium, and chloride plus exchange behavior make supplier processing and batch testing important. Do not assume every washed or buffered claim has the same analytical meaning.
Use media pH/EC, irrigation analysis, tissue data, and input history alongside CEC. A percentage ratio is not a substitute for crop response and total concentration.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Media components, supplier, lot, and declared processing.
CEC method, units, pH basis, and sampling date.
Ca, Mg, K, Na, acidity, and other reported values.
Input and root-zone pH/EC with extraction method.
Tissue analysis, symptoms, growth, and corrective action.

misconceptions: High CEC means high fertility: Capacity is not the same as balanced occupancy or plant availability.
CEC controls anions and cations equally: Conventional CEC specifically describes cation exchange.
One ideal base-saturation ratio fits every substrate: Crop, method, mineralogy, pH, and total supply matter.
evidenceLimits: CEC tests developed for mineral soils may not translate directly to soilless substrates. Compare values only when sample preparation, method, and units match.
